newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Modest UK sales seen easing boom fears.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Modest UK sales seen easing boom fears.

text.p: British retail sales are forecast to have risen just 0.1 percent in May, which would help to allay fears of a runaway high street boom, analysts said on Monday.

A Reuter poll of economists found a consensus forecasting meagre sales growth last month, leaving sales 4.4 percent higher than they were a year ago. The figures will be released at 0830 GMT on Wednesday.
One problem facing forecasters is the conflicting evidence offered by the Confederation of British Industry and British Retail Consortium for last month.
The CBI's May distributive trades survey showed the lowest annual rate of sales increase since October 1995 but the BRC's sales monitor was much more bullish.
It showed retail sales grew 4.8 percent year-on-year in May, in value terms, up from 4.1 in April.
If in doubt, bet on the BRC, Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said.
"Whenever the CBI and BRC disagree, the official sales data tend to move with the BRC numbers," he said. "We expect a 0.3 percent rise, leaving the annual rate unchanged (at 4.7 percent)."

Darshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets, said weekly sales figure from department store group the John Lewis Partnership suggested a small rise in overall retail sales, although she forecast flat sales on the month.
"As sales have now risen for four consecutive months, this would hardly be surprising and, indeed, would help to quell fears of a windfall-led boom," she said.
Building societies converting into banks are expected to hand over shares worth a staggering 35 billion pounds to millions of members over the summer.
Halifax Plc has already floated on the stock exchange and issued windfall shares worth 17 billion pounds or more.
But even if high street spending did not increase at all last month, the underlying trend remains firm.
Flat sales growth in May still tranaslates into a 4.3 percent annual increase. "And with the three-month-on-three-month rate of 1.2 percent, the trend in sales remains very robust," David said.
Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, also said recent months had seen solid sales growth all the way.
Only in value terms have sales eased back and that is because high street inflation has eased back, not because the volume of goods sold has dropped.
"We expect this trend to continue," Saunders said. "Retailers are responding to any weakness in nominal spending growth by squeezing prices."
David agreed, saying: "The retail sales deflator has fallen over recent months...and this bodes well for inflation pressures remaining subdued at the retail level."
Underlying retail prices rose 2.5 percent in the year to May, bang on the government's target.
